12.0.s.en: 1. God's mercies in the midst of His wrath:

12.0.0.en: "And in that day thou shalt say, O Lord, I will praise thee: though thou wast angry with me, thine anger is turned away, and thou comfortedst me." [1].

12.0.1.en: The new song uttered by everyone who enjoys the saving work of the Lord Christ begins with the words: "And in that day thou shalt say." Which day is this? It is the day of the Cross, or the great Day of Atonement, on which we praise the Lord who turned wrath into salvation, comfort and glory. The divine wrath against the sin we commit took form in the crucifixion of the Lord Christ, the incarnate Word of God, to lift us from wrath to glory. The wonderful comforts of God appeared when He freed us, not from the Babylonian captivity, but from the captivity of the devil and his hosts and his evil works, that righteousness might reign in us.

12.0.2.en: Thus we offer praise and thanksgiving to God, not like the Pharisee who stood in the temple boasting over others, but like the thief on the right, driven outside the camp for his sins, who finds in his company the Lord Christ crucified for his sake, opening to him the gates of Paradise. So God's wrath against us turns into surpassing heavenly and divine comforts. On that day He Himself became our peace (Eph 2:14), and in Him God reconciled the world unto Himself (2 Cor 5:19).

12.1.s.en: 2. Yahweh, the secret of our salvation, strength and joy:

12.1.0.en: "Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and not be afraid: for the Lord Jehovah is my strength and my song; he also is become my salvation." "Therefore with joy shall ye draw water out of the wells of salvation." [2-3].

12.1.1.en: The Coptic Church took a portion of this hymn to chant it to the crucified Lord on Covenant Thursday and Good Friday, namely: "My strength and my song (my hymn) is the Lord, and He is become my salvation. God is the secret of our strength, our praise and our salvation! In the midst of her sharing in her Bridegroom's sufferings the Church praises and sings; and her song or hymn is Christ Himself, who is everything to her.

12.1.2.en: Through the crucified Christ we have come to know the joyful sound (Ps 89:15); the shout of victory over the devil and his evil works! The shout of salvation by which we pass from the left to the right and enjoy the fellowship of the joyful heavenly Kingdom.

12.1.3.en: By the Cross a fountain of blood and water burst forth from the pierced side that we might be sanctified and cleansed, but also that we might drink and rejoice, for we have found the fountain of our eternal salvation.

12.1.4.en: Here he calls God "Yah Yahweh" (the Lord Jehovah); "Yah" is an abbreviation of the name "Yahweh," as though the hymn repeats this divine title "Yahweh" to affirm that He is the eternal God who does not change, on whom the believer leans, finding in Him his strength, his joy and his salvation forever, so that he is always at peace without fear. As St. Augustine says: [If you wish your joy to be steadfast and lasting, cling to the eternal God, to Him in whom no change occurs, but who continues steadfast in one state forever.]

12.2.s.en: 3. Witness to the works of God:

12.2.0.en: 4 And in that day shall ye say, "Praise the Lord, call upon his name, declare his doings among the people, make mention that his name is exalted. 5 Sing unto the Lord; for he hath done excellent things: this is known in all the earth. 6 Cry out and shout, thou inhabitant of Zion: for great is the Holy One of Israel in the midst of thee."

12.2.1.en: Some see the preceding phrases [1-3] as representing a hymn independent of the phrases that follow [4-6], which represent a second hymn. In any case, if the first announces the springing up of praise and thanksgiving in the soul through the enjoyment of the Lord's salvation, the second completes it, announcing the obligation to bear witness to God the Savior before the nations. For what we experience through our union with God our Savior stirs in us a longing that others enjoy the same salvation. "And in that day shall ye say, Praise the Lord, call upon his name, declare his doings among the people, make mention that his name is exalted. Sing unto the Lord; for he hath done excellent things: this is known in all the earth. Cry out and shout, thou inhabitant of Zion: for great is the Holy One of Israel in the midst of thee" [4-6].

12.2.2.en: How do we preach the Lord?

12.2.3.en: A. By evangelism: "declare his doings among the people," as the Lord says to His disciples: "Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature" (Mk 16:5). Every believer is bound to bear witness to his Savior, for we see the psalmist David, declaring his repentance in the fiftieth Psalm, saying: "Grant me the joy of thy salvation, and I will teach sinners thy ways."

12.2.4.en: B. By holy joy: "Sing unto the Lord; for he hath done excellent things: this is known in all the earth." There is no greater witness to the Savior than others' touching our inner joy in the Lord, which passes through all events and troubles. The psalmist says: "Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing: then said they among the nations, The Lord hath done great things for us" (Ps 26:2).

12.2.5.en: The voice of inner rejoicing bears witness to the dwelling of the Holy One in us!

12.2.6.en: Holy joy proclaims the joyful Kingdom of God within us. It is told in the life of St. Apollo the priest in Thebes, on the borders of Hermopolis (Ashmunein), that his face was always cheerful, thereby drawing many to the ascetic life as a life joyful within and satisfying the heart with the Lord Himself. He often repeated the saying: [Why do we strive with sullen faces?! Are we not heirs of eternal life? Leave gloom and sullenness to the pagans and wailing to the sinners (the wicked); but for the righteous and the saints it is fitting that they rejoice and smile, because they enjoy spiritual things.]

13.0.0.en: "The oracle concerning Babylon, which Isaiah the son of Amoz did see:" [1].

13.0.1.en: The prophet wished to affirm that he is the writer of the prophecy, and enjoyed it concerning Babylon. His affirmation that he is the one who saw it is for two reasons:

13.0.2.en: A. Although Isaiah prophesied concerning Judah and Jerusalem, he speaks here of the fate of the neighboring nations, affirming that the God of the saints is the very God of all nations.

13.0.3.en: B. Babylon was of no account at that time, so it was hard for the hearer or reader to believe what is said of it in these prophecies.

13.0.4.en: The word "oracle" came in Hebrew as massâh, and it was translated in the Targum, the Vulgate and the Syriac version with the meaning of "load" or "burden," perhaps because the prophet himself, by reason of his tenderness, felt a heavy and bitter burden over the troubles and divine disciplines that would come upon these nations. Even if these disciplines were deserved and would in the end turn to good, the prophet, as a man of God, does not stand gloating but grieving. In this spirit the early Church lived, disciplining, but in love and gentleness, not closing the door of repentance before sinners, even those who denied the faith. They counted men like Novatian heretics because of their harshness toward sinners. As St. Ambrose says in his reply to him: [By this they have passed sentence on the corruption of their teaching, for by denying the authority to loose they have denied their authority to bind also... What more shall I say of their increasing arrogance? For their will is contrary to the will of the Spirit of the Lord, who inclines to mercy and not to harshness... They do what He does not will. For He is the Judge and has the right to punish, yet we find Him by His mercy pardoning...! We must know that God is a God of mercy, inclined to pardon and not to harshness. Therefore it was said: "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice" (Hos 6:6); how then will God accept your offerings, you who deny mercy, when it has been said of God that He does not will the death of the sinner so much as that he return (Ezek 18:32)?]

13.0.5.en: Some scholars think that what is said about Babylon in the two chapters (13, 14) is not the work of the prophet Isaiah, and their arguments for this are:

13.0.6.en: A. That Babylon was bound in friendship with Judah (Isa 39), so how could he proclaim a harsh prophecy against it?!

13.0.7.en: B. Babylon was subject to Assyria in weakness.

13.0.8.en: C. It appears from the discourse that Israel was in captivity to Babylon at the time the prophecy was proclaimed.

13.0.9.en: The answer to this is that the prophet was speaking of the future by the spirit of prophecy, pointing to the discipline of Israel by Assyria, then the position of Babylon afterwards when Assyria was shattered and Babylon became a great kingdom, and the captivity of the people and then their return, and finally the coming of the Savior Immanuel in the fullness of time. The prophet speaks of the future as a present he is living, and this is a natural thing the prophets were accustomed to, to affirm that what they proclaim will be fulfilled exactly. Nor do we ignore that the prophet who gave precise details about the person of the Lord Christ, His life, His saving work and the marks of His age, can prophesy the rise of the Babylonian state and the captivity of the people by it, which took place about 100 years after the proclamation of the prophecy. The prophet Jeremiah later, during the Babylonian era, echoed the very cries of Isaiah.

13.0.10.en: Finally, the prophet's speaking of the return from the captivity (Isa 11) and his threatening of the Babylonian captivity (Isa 39) indicates that the matter of the Babylonian captivity was not far from the mind of the prophet Isaiah.

13.1.s.en: 2. A call to the nations to fight Babylon:

13.1.0.en: 2 Lift ye up a banner upon the bare mountain, exalt the voice unto them, shake the hand, that they may go into the gates of the tyrants. 3 I have commanded my sanctified ones, I have also called my mighty ones for mine anger, even them that rejoice in my highness. 4 The noise of a multitude in the mountains, like as of a great people; a tumultuous noise of the kingdoms of nations gathered together: the Lord of hosts mustereth the host of the battle. 5 They come from a far country, from the end of heaven, even the Lord, and the weapons of his indignation, to destroy the whole land.

13.1.1.en: The greatness of Babylon had not yet appeared, but the prophet sees it coming, its capital a city of tyrants, and so he begins his prophecy about it with the Lord's inciting the nations to throng together against Babylon, to storm its gates and humble its pride, saying:

13.1.2.en: "Lift ye up a banner upon the bare mountain" [2]. Thus God issues a command to make war on Babylon, calling the nations to raise the banner of war on a mountain empty of every tree or plant so that the whole army can see it. It was the custom in ancient times for some soldiers to gather wood and kindle it by night on the mountain as a sign of the beginning of war; so their being on a mountain without trees helps the army quickly notice the beginning of the war.

13.1.3.en: "Exalt the voice unto them" [2], that is, sound the trumpets to rouse the armies.

13.1.4.en: "Shake the hand, that they may go into the gates of the tyrants (the nobles)" [2], that is, they wave their hands to encourage resolve for storming the city of the free nobles with courage and boldness.

13.1.5.en: What is Babylon but the arrogant soul, which we must storm, not with banners of war, nor with the sound of trumpets, nor with the waving of human hands, but by raising the banner of love that belongs to our crucified Christ, so that it says: "His banner over me was love" (Song 2:4). Let us blow the trumpet of the Gospel, joyful to souls, and let us stretch out the hand of practical love to support the weak soul that pride has humbled... Thus we storm the soul by the Spirit of the Lord working in us, and draw it to the account of His heavenly Kingdom through spiritual warfare made effective by divine grace and not by human work.

13.2.0.en: The discourse here is greater than a call to Persia and Media to storm the great empire of Babylon; it is a call that touches the eternal salvation of the soul. Therefore he goes on to say: "I have commanded my sanctified ones, I have also called my mighty ones for mine anger, even them that rejoice in my highness. The noise of a multitude in the mountains, like as of a great people; a tumultuous noise of the kingdoms of nations gathered together: the Lord of hosts mustereth the host of the battle. They come from a far country, from the end of heaven, even the Lord, and the weapons of his indignation, to destroy the land" [3-5].

13.2.2.en: First: who are these sanctified ones and mighty ones belonging to God who are used in this battle? Some see them as the military leaders of Persia and Media, who were called to a holy battle, not because they were saints in their life or faith, but because God called them, without their knowing, to accomplish His holy purposes, and gave them power to work and used them to accomplish things that were not in their thoughts. They were counted God's mighty ones in spite of their unbelief in Him, just as Cyrus the pagan was called the anointed of the Lord, whose right hand God held, to tread down nations before him, and so on... (Isa 45:1).

13.2.3.en: Such is the wonderful goodness of God, who turns the energies and works even of the wicked to the account of the growth of His Kingdom and the building up of souls.

13.2.4.en: If God called the pagan stormers of Babylon His sanctified ones and His mighty ones, what then is the state of His children, the "spiritual soldiers," who are truly the saints of the Lord, since they are set apart for holy spiritual work, who fight against the devil and all his evil works for the sanctification of their own depths and the sanctification of others by winning them with divine love; He also calls them "His mighty ones" because they carry His strength and work by His Holy Spirit; and He also counts them "them that rejoice in my highness," since they accomplish the glory of the great name of God.

13.2.5.en: The holy Fathers see Baptism as an entrance into spiritual soldiery, where the candidate for baptism is sealed with the seal of the Spirit and is counted a spiritual soldier for the Lord's kingdom.

13.2.6.en: * Each one of you comes and presents himself before God in the presence of countless armies of angels, and the Holy Spirit sets a mark on your souls. By this you enroll yourselves in the army of the great King.

13.2.7.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem * As the seal is stamped on soldiers, so the Holy Spirit is stamped on believers.

13.2.8.en: St. John Chrysostom * He who receives the bath of regeneration is like a young soldier who has been given a place among the combatants but has not yet proved his worthiness for soldiering.

13.2.9.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa Second: what is the voice of the multitude standing on the mountains like a great people, "a tumultuous noise of the kingdoms of nations gathered together: the Lord of hosts mustereth the host of the battle" (Isa 43:4), but the voice of the Church gathered together in a spirit of love and unity on the holy mountains, enjoying the life on high, dwelling on the summits of the blessed commandments and not at the foot, gathered from the kingdoms of many nations as an army with banners (Song 6:10)... They are many churches with differing cultures, but through one faith and one mind they live as a heavenly spiritual army... This is the mark of the true Church: a heavenly Church! Therefore the Apostle Paul says: "But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord" (2 Cor 3:18).

13.2.10.en: * How many have attacked the Church, and those who attacked it have perished, while she has soared into heaven.

13.2.11.en: * The Church is your hope, your salvation and your refuge. She is higher than heaven and wider than the world.

13.3.0.en: St. John Chrysostom "They come from a far country, from the end of heaven, even the Lord, and the weapons of his indignation, to destroy the whole land" [5]. The Church is gathered from a far country, for most of her members were pagans bound to the world, strangers to the house of God, but they became the heaven of the Lord and His sanctuary, destroying temporal thoughts or the love of earthly things, to carry others to the experience of the heavenly life. It is as though the destruction of the earth means the shattering of the closing of the heart upon temporal things so that it opens to heaven. As St. Clement of Alexandria says, the earth becomes heaven for the believer (the gnostic).

13.3.1.en: This is from the symbolic side; but from the literal side, God called the nations of Persia and Media and others to use them to destroy the whole land of great Babylon.

13.4.0.en: 6 Howl ye; for the day of the Lord is at hand; it shall come as a destruction from the Almighty. 7 Therefore shall all hands be faint, and every man's heart shall melt: 8 And they shall be afraid: pangs and sorrows shall take hold of them; they shall be in pain as a woman that travaileth: they shall be amazed one at another; their faces shall be as flames. 9 Behold, the day of the Lord cometh, cruel both with wrath and fierce anger, to lay the land desolate: and he shall destroy the sinners thereof out of it. 10 For the stars of heaven and the mighty ones thereof shall not give their light: the sun shall be darkened in his going forth, and the moon shall not cause her light to shine. 11 And I will punish the world for their evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; and I will cause the arrogancy of the proud to cease, and will lay low the haughtiness of the tyrants. 12 I will make a man more precious than fine gold; even a man than the golden wedge of Ophir. 13 Therefore I will shake the heavens, and the earth shall remove out of her place, in the wrath of the Lord of hosts, and in the day of his fierce anger. 14 And it shall be as the chased roe, and as a sheep that no man taketh up: they shall every man turn to his own people, and flee every one into his own land. 15 Every one that is found shall be thrust through; and every one that is joined unto them shall fall by the sword. 16 Their children also shall be dashed to pieces before their eyes; their houses shall be spoiled, and their wives ravished. 17 Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them, which shall not regard silver; and as for gold, they shall not delight in it. 18 Their bows also shall dash the young men to pieces; and they shall have no pity on the fruit of the womb; their eyes shall not spare children. 19 And Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the beauty of the Chaldees' excellency, shall be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah. 20 It shall never be inhabited, neither shall it be dwelt in from generation to generation: neither shall the Arabian pitch tent there; neither shall the shepherds make their fold there. 21 But wild beasts of the desert shall lie there; and owls shall fill their houses, and ostriches shall dwell there, and wild goats shall dance there. 22 And jackals shall cry in their palaces, and wolves in the temples of pleasure: and her time is near to come, and her days shall not be prolonged.

13.4.1.en: The prophet portrays for us the dreadful day of Babylon's destruction at the hands of Persia and Media as the day of the Lord, on which He declares His wrath against Babylon, which resisted Him and His children.

13.4.2.en: This was fulfilled at the hands of Cyrus, who was not cruel, but his army was violent, savage and barbarous; therefore the soldiers destroyed Babylon not so much to plunder its treasures as from a desire to shed blood.

13.4.3.en: Some see that what is stated here was indeed fulfilled in the days of Cyrus but only in part, though it will be fulfilled more fully in the last days, as the Book of Revelation (Rev 17) speaks of the judgment of the great harlot who sits upon many waters, Babylon the great, the mother of harlots.

13.4.4.en: I say that this prophecy announces what is accomplished with respect to the kingdom of the devil, not only in the last days but in the heart of every person who accepts faith in the Lord Christ as King, who establishes a new Jerusalem in him in place of the harlot Babylon, that is, establishes His holy city in place of the kingdom of the devil.

13.4.5.en: A. The prophet says: "Howl ye; for the day of the Lord is at hand; it shall come as a destruction from the Almighty. Therefore shall all hands be faint" [6], so that they have no strength to carry weapons. The kingdom of Babylon had become mistress of the whole world; God had been long-suffering toward it for tens of years, while the Babylonians went on in the pride of their hearts and their arrogance against the Lord Himself; therefore when they fall under His wrath their violent weapon-bearing hands grow faint, and they become very weak and an object of mockery.

13.4.6.en: This is the picture of the enemy of good as St. John Chrysostom disclosed it in his letter to his friend Theodore the fallen, explaining to him that the devil appears extremely violent and possessed of power and might, but when we carry our Christ he grows weak and collapses. And in an article on: "The power of man to resist Satan he says: [Satan is wicked, and I concede that, but he is wicked toward himself and not toward us so long as we are watchful, for such is the nature of evil, it is destructive only to those who cling to it alone"].

13.5.0.en: B. "And every man's heart shall melt: and they shall be afraid" [7-8]. Thus a state of trembling and fear seizes all, men and women, young and old and children; all become shattered, none supports his brother, but each one breaks himself as he breaks those around him!

13.5.1.en: The secret of their trembling is their being deprived of the fear of God. He who fears God fears neither man nor events but is filled with joy and peace; therefore it was said: "The head of wisdom is the fear of God." St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian says: [Let the fear of God be in your heart, beloved, like the weapon in the hand of the soldier.]

13.6.0.en: C. "They shall be in pain as a woman that travaileth" [8], for they carried within them the fruit of evil, which they bring forth in bitterness upon bitterness. And the wonder is that the Holy Bible likens the pains of the wicked to the pains of labor, and also the pains of the believers (Jn 16:20); the former groan in despair and in trembling because they bring forth wind (Isa 26:18), while the latter rejoice in the midst of outward sorrow because they bring a man into the world (Jn 16:20).

13.6.1.en: D. "Your faces shall be as flames" [8], red with shame because of their utter brokenness and their cowardice, as their faces sometimes grow pale [8], turning yellow with fear.

13.7.0.en: E. "To lay the land desolate, with none to walk upon it" [9], as a symbol of what befalls the body (the earth) in the loss of all true vitality. He who resists the Lord for the sake of the lusts of the body loses even his body and his inner soul is laid waste, for it was said: "Therefore I will shake the heavens (the soul), and the earth (the body) shall remove out of her place, in the wrath" [13]. Perhaps here he also points to nature's rebellion against the one who disobeys its Creator. It is as though nature itself disobeys the one who disobeys the Lord!

13.8.0.en: F. Darkness comes upon them: "For the stars of heaven and the mighty ones thereof shall not give their light: the sun shall be darkened in his going forth, and the moon shall not cause her light to shine" [10]. This points to the darkness of ignorance that comes upon the man who resists God, for he does not see the light of the heavenly bodies, all of them, including the sun and the moon. He does not see the Sun of righteousness, that is, faith in Christ, who is able to give him wisdom and knowledge; nor does he see the light of the moon, that is, the Church life enlightened by the Lord, as the moon bearing the reflections of the light of the sun; nor does he enjoy the light of the other stars, or fellowship with the saints who shine as luminous stars.

13.9.0.en: G. The men die in the war, and since the women of Babylon were accustomed to a licentious life, they seek a man to fulfill their evil lusts, and it is hard for them to find one: "I will make a man more precious than fine gold; even a man than the golden wedge of Ophir (perhaps a region in the southeast of Arabia or a place on the west coast of India)" [12]. This also points to the scarcity of laborers because of the war, with the return of the captives and the liberation of the nations from the Babylonian authority.

13.10.0.en: H. The loss of leadership and shepherding: "And it shall be as the chased roe, and as a sheep that no man taketh up: they shall every man turn to his own people, and flee every one into his own land" [14]. He means that on the day of Babylon's defeat the army loses its leadership, and the hired soldiers, or those conscripted from the nations, flee each to his own country.

13.10.1.en: This is the state of the soul far from God, for it loses its inner leadership, so that man lives as one chased, or as sheep with no shepherd to gather them... He carries within him bitter conflicts and a scattering of thought, with a shattering of inner energies.

13.11.0.en: I. Slaughter of all without distinction between soldier or civilian, man, woman or child [15]. Here he depicts what the Medes do against Babylon, for the Medes do not destroy it to acquire wealth [17] but to destroy all of Babylon's energies, so they pay no regard to a small youth or to a child in his mother's womb [18]; they ruin all its resources, so that it becomes like Sodom and Gomorrah, which were burned with fire from heaven.

13.11.1.en: J. Babylon becomes an everlasting wilderness; no Arab shepherding his flock dwells in it, nor do shepherds lie down in it for fear of the beasts of prey that inhabit it (Isa 30:20-21). It becomes a ruin in which owls dwell in what remains of the houses, and there are in it ostriches, wild goats, jackals and wolves.

13.11.2.en: Father Serenus says: [We must not take all these names haphazardly, but they point to the ferocity (of the demons) and their madness under the symbol of predatory beasts, as being harmful and dangerous... and more evil than they.]

13.11.3.en: It is a picture of the soul that surrenders to the enemy of good, so that he uses it for the account of the kingdom of darkness, fills it with evil and turns it into a factory of corruption:

13.12.0.en: "But wild beasts of the desert shall lie there" [21]... Violence dwells in it, and ferocity, and the love of shedding innocent blood without cause.

13.12.1.en: "And owls shall fill their houses" [21], where most Easterners take their voices as an ill omen... It is as though nothing is heard within the wicked man but the voices of despair and pessimism, which reveal an inner emptiness.

13.12.2.en: "And ostriches shall dwell there" [21], that is, it is full of uncleanness (Lev 11:16; Deut 14:15), its voice like wailing (Mic 1:8); heavenly joy does not enter it, its nature is dry, it does not love its eggs (Lam 4:3); it buries its head in the sand when it sees a hunter approaching it, and it used to be thought that it does this because it supposes that thereby the hunter does not see it, but it has recently been shown that it does this because it is too cowardly to see itself fall victim to the hunters.

13.12.3.en: "And wild goats shall dance there" [21]. Perhaps it means the ibex, found only in desolate places. So the demons dance and sport in the wicked soul, since they find a place for themselves in it.

13.13.0.en: "And jackals (an animal larger than a fox and smaller than a wolf) shall cry in their palaces, and wolves in the temples of pleasure" [22]... that is, the palaces and temples are turned from places of pleasure into a refuge for fierce beasts.

13.13.1.en: All this came upon Babylon, "the glory of kingdoms, the beauty of the Chaldees' excellency" [19], the golden city (Isa 14:4), rich in its treasures (Jer 51:13), the glory of all the earth (Jer 51:41), likened to the head of gold in the statue mentioned in the Book of Daniel. The prophecies were fulfilled in it literally as they were stated, for history records that Cyrus tore down a large part of the walls and buildings of Babylon, and after 20 years Darius pulled down the rest of the walls and removed its bronze gates and crucified three thousand of its notables. It is said that the length of the wall of Babylon was 60 miles, 15 miles on each side, its height 300 feet and its thickness 80 feet, so that six chariots could drive side by side on the wall. Its depth in the ground was 35 feet so that the enemy could not dig a way for himself beneath it, and 250 towers for watching and guarding stood upon the wall, and it had 100 huge, shining bronze gates.

13.13.2.en: Babylon was indeed turned to ruin, and Alexander the Great tried to restore its glory but died before carrying out his projects. Its stones were used in building Baghdad, repairing canals and erecting many public facilities.

13.13.3.en: Finally, the prophet affirmed that what he says is quickly fulfilled: "And her time is near to come, and her days shall not be prolonged" [22]. The star of Babylon began to shine in 606 B.C., and it fell into the hands of Persia and Media in 536 B.C., while the prophecy came in the eighth century B.C.

13.13.4.en: Babylon has remained a symbol of every proud, rebellious soul, as the Book of Revelation has it, where it was said: "For in one hour is thy judgment come" (Rev 18:10).
